headline: OGDC profit rises 53pc to Rs58.5b in first quarter
description: ISLAMABAD - Oil & Gas Development Company Limited (OGDC), Pakistan’s largest exploration and production company, on Friday reported a profit after
author: PR
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - Oil & Gas Development Company Limited (OGDC), Pakistan’s largest exploration and production company, on Friday reported a profit after tax of Rs58.5 billion for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, an increase of 53 percent over the corresponding quarter last year. The Board of Directors, at its meeting in Islamabad, approved the financial results and declared a first interim cash dividend of Rs5.00 per share (50 percent), the highest first-quarter dividend in the company’s history, up from Rs3.50 per share a year earlier.

Net sales revenue rose 38 percent to Rs132.4 billion from Rs96.2 billion in the corresponding quarter, and profit after tax increased to Rs58.5 billion from Rs38.3 billion, lifting earnings per share to Rs13.60 from Rs8.91. The improvement was driven by higher production volumes and stronger realised prices, partly offset by continued forced production curtailments and the appreciation of the rupee against the US dollar. Collections against billings stood at 100 percent for the quarter. OGDC contributed Rs82 billion to the national exchequer through taxes, dividends, royalties and levies, and its indigenous oil and gas production saved the country an estimated $1.32 billion in foreign exchange through import substitution.

Commenting on the results, Zafar Masud, Chairman of the Board, said: “This was a quarter of delivery: double-digit growth in oil, gas and LPG production, collections at 100 percent of billings, and a record first-quarter dividend for our shareholders. The board’s decision reflects confidence in the company’s cash generation, while preserving its capacity to invest in compression, water injection and new drilling to sustain production and to pursue new frontiers in unconventional gas, geothermal energy and critical minerals.” Production grew in all three streams. Average daily net saleable production rose 13.3 percent to 35,494 barrels of crude oil, 14.2 percent to 732 MMcf of natural gas and 10.5 percent to 696 tonnes of LPG, compared with 31,315 barrels, 641 MMcf and 630 tonnes, respectively, in the corresponding quarter last year.

Growth was supported by the connection of four new wells—Maru-3, Sono-10, Chak 63-5 and Bobi-11—to the production gathering system. Electrical submersible pumps installed at four wells added 1,630 barrels per day of crude oil. The company also completed 26 workover jobs to sustain production and arrest natural decline in mature fields. Forced production curtailments by SNGPL and UPL continued to constrain output, reducing average daily net production by 1,254 barrels of crude oil, 94 MMcf of gas and five tonnes of LPG, at an estimated cost of Rs9.7 billion in sales revenue. This compares with Rs19.3 billion in the corresponding quarter last year. Without these curtailments, average daily net production would have been 36,748 barrels of crude oil, 826 MMcf of gas and 701 tonnes of LPG.

Average realised crude oil and gas prices increased to $74.90 per barrel and Rs796.08 per Mcf, respectively, compared with $57.61 per barrel and Rs718.38 per Mcf in the corresponding period. On the exploration front, OGDC acquired 31 line-km of 2D and 213 sq km of 3D seismic data. Seismic acquisition was affected by security constraints, adverse weather and supply chain disruptions. The company spudded Bitrism NW-1 and Nahiyoon-1 and achieved total drilling footage of 17,348 metres. Nahiyoon-1, a horizontal pilot well targeting the Sembar shale, marks OGDC’s first step in assessing Pakistan’s unconventional gas potential, alongside an ongoing regional tight gas evaluation study.

Investment to sustain production and improve recovery continued. Construction and mechanical works on the Uch Compression Project are complete, with commissioning underway and performance testing to be completed in stages by December 2026. The KPD-TAY Compression Project is at an advanced stage and targeted for completion by March 2027, as is the Kunnar-Pasakhi Water Injection Project, the company’s first step towards systematic enhanced oil recovery, which is expected to improve recovery by 8-10 percent and extend the economic life of the fields by seven to eight years. Work is also progressing on the Rajian Heavy Oil Facility Project and a mature asset revitalisation initiative targeting additional recovery and longer asset life.

The company continued to advance its diversification initiatives. In Abu Dhabi Offshore Block-5, exploration and appraisal studies are underway, alongside front-end engineering design for the development of Bu Dana, Al Bateen and Al Manhal fields, with first production targeted for 2028. At Reko Diq, the operator is reviewing the project’s security situation, capital requirements, financing, scope and timelines, which may result in changes to estimated costs and schedules. OGDC remains engaged with the operator, co-shareholders and the government on this strategic investment.

OGDC has identified lithium in geothermal brine at Wahid Bakhsh-1, with laboratory analysis by PINSTECH recording a concentration of 291 mg/L, a level comparable to leading geothermal-lithium brines internationally. These are preliminary findings: assessment of lithium potential in adjacent water formations and of the commercial viability of geothermal resources is underway and will inform future development plans.

During the quarter, the board approved OGDC’s first sustainability-related financial disclosures prepared in accordance with IFRS S1 and IFRS S2. The company also established directorate-wise performance indicators and measurable targets under its board-approved ESG strategy and conducted an ESG awareness session for supply chain partners. These measures support its commitments under the Oil and Gas Decarbonisation Charter and the UN Environment Programme’s Oil and Gas Methane Partnership 2.0, which OGDC was the first Pakistani company to join.

OGDC’s governance standards were recognised in Transparency International Pakistan’s Transparency in Corporate Reporting (TRAC) Assessment 2026, in which the Company ranked first among 104 listed companies across 28 sectors with an overall score of 92.71 percent. It scored 100 percent in Anti-Corruption Programmes, Organisational Transparency, Domestic Financial Reporting, and Gender, Disability and Non-Discrimination, as well as in the separately assessed Procurement category. The assessment is based on publicly available disclosures.

OGDC remains focused on sustaining production, improving recovery from mature fields, advancing exploration and development, and maintaining financial discipline, so that it continues to deliver for its shareholders and for Pakistan’s energy security.

headline: PC Hospitality partners with Organiks Plus to promote sustainable hospitality, eliminate single-use plastics
description: ISLAMABAD - PC Hospitality, the hospitality division of Hashoo Group, has joined hands with Organiks Plus, a women-led social enterprise established by the
author: PR
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - PC Hospitality, the hospitality division of Hashoo Group, has joined hands with Organiks Plus, a women-led social enterprise established by the Hashoo Foundation, to advance sustainable hospitality practices through the adoption of locally manufactured toiletries and innovative “forever vanity set” across its entire portfolio.

The collaboration reflects PC Hospitality’s commitment to reducing its environmental footprint while supporting local enterprise and women’s economic empowerment. By introducing these permanent, high-end wall mounted solutions in place of conventional single-use plastic toiletries, the initiative aims to eliminate plastic waste and encourage more responsible consumption throughout its hotel operations.

Currently progressing through a structured, gradual deployment across the network, with over 60 percent of the portfolio already successfully transitioned, the initiative spans all PC Hospitality brands, including Pearl-Continental Hotels & Resorts, PC Signature Collection, PC Legacy, PC Residences, and Hotel One. From luxury destinations to select-service properties, this seamless integration demonstrates that environmentally responsible practices can be adopted consistently without compromising guest comfort, hygiene, or quality.

Through this collaboration, PC Hospitality is incorporating Organiks Plus’s locally manufactured personal care products into the guest experience, reducing reliance on disposable packaging while promoting efficient resource utilisation. Beyond environmental sustainability, the collaboration carries a broader social purpose, supporting local communities, promoting indigenous products, and creating economic opportunities for women and youth.

Commenting on the initiative, Bastien Blanc, CEO of PC Hospitality, said:

“Sustainability is an integral part of how we envision the future of hospitality. Our collaboration with Organiks Plus allows us to take meaningful steps towards eliminating single-use plastics through our forever dispensers while supporting local manufacturing and women’s economic empowerment. By extending this initiative across our portfolio, with over 60 percent already deployed, we are demonstrating that responsible business practices and exceptional guest experiences go hand in hand.”

Commenting on the collaboration, Sumeira Hashwani, CEO of Organiks Plus, said:

“At Organiks Plus, we believe that empowering households and enriching communities go hand in hand with building a strong, competitive local economy. Our vision is to create opportunities for local producers and communities while developing high-quality products that meet international standards and compete confidently with global brands. This collaboration reflects our belief that locally manufactured products can deliver exceptional quality while creating meaningful economic opportunities and contributing to a more sustainable future.”

headline: Ahsan Iqbal orders removal of bottlenecks in NHA projects, warns against cost escalations
description: ISLAMABAD - Federal Planning, Development and Special Initiatives Minister Ahsan Iqbal on Friday directed the National Highway Authority (NHA) to remove
author: Fawad Yousafzai
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - Federal Planning, Development and Special Initiatives Minister Ahsan Iqbal on Friday directed the National Highway Authority (NHA) to remove bottlenecks in ongoing development projects and warned that unjustified cost escalations, non-transparent financial claims and weak project oversight will not be tolerated.

While reviewing NHA projects under the Public Sector Development Programme (PSDP), the minister directed the authority to accelerate work on key national highways and motorways and ensure transparent and efficient utilisation of public funds.

He emphasised that the development budget is public money and must be used with financial discipline and accountability. He directed thorough scrutiny of cost escalations, variations in construction quantities and rates, and additional claims by contractors to prevent unnecessary burden on the exchequer.

Stressing effective monitoring, Ahsan Iqbal said oversight must focus on actual physical progress, expenditure and completion targets, not just paperwork. He directed the authorities to prepare a comprehensive report on the status, financial requirements and implementation bottlenecks of key projects for submission to the Prime Minister to facilitate timely decisions.

Reviewing major highway projects, the minister was informed that the 216-kilometre Shandur–Gilgit Road, costing Rs49,946.070 million, has achieved 67.33 percent progress, while the 153-kilometre Chitral–Booni–Mastuj–Shandur Road, costing Rs17,783.193 million, has achieved 40 percent progress. He stressed accelerating these strategically important routes to improve connectivity in remote areas.

The 273-kilometre dualisation and rehabilitation of the Karachi–Quetta–Chaman Road (N-25), costing Rs183,421.427 million, has achieved 19.25 percent progress. The minister underlined the importance of accelerating this corridor, including the Karachi–Kararo and Wadh–Khuzdar sections, to strengthen connectivity and trade. Regarding the Indus Highway, the 221.9-kilometre Shikarpur–Rajanpur Additional Carriageway on N-55, costing Rs44,703.890 million, has achieved 62 percent progress. The 121.5-kilometre Rajanpur–Dera Ghazi Khan section, costing Rs63,150.570 million, is awaiting letters of award due to land acquisition issues. The 208.19-kilometre Dera Ghazi Khan–Dera Ismail Khan section, costing Rs111,940.070 million, has been awarded and contractors are under mobilisation. He directed to resolve outstanding issues and accelerate work.

The 306-kilometre Hyderabad–Sukkur Motorway (M-6), costing Rs363,700 million, and the electrical and mechanical works of the Lowari Tunnel, costing Rs33,250 million, are at the procurement stage. Ahsan Iqbal directed removal of procedural bottlenecks to expedite procurement. The 210-kilometre dualisation of N-50 from Yarik through Sagu to Zhob, including Zhob Bypass, costing Rs76,486.231 million, has achieved 10 percent progress. He directed acceleration and addressing financial constraints.

Highlighting the importance of M-6, N-55, N-25 and Quetta–Zhob networks, the minister said their timely completion was essential for economic growth, trade and regional connectivity. He called for practical strategies, clear timelines and effective coordination. He directed that all exceptional cost escalations and financial claims undergo thorough technical, contractual and financial scrutiny. Engineers, project directors and consultants must discharge responsibilities effectively, while monitoring and accountability mechanisms should be strengthened.

He also underscored independent third-party validation to assess costs, quality and quantities, saying verification must be impartial and free from conflict of interest. He further directed identification of projects that could be completed with limited additional allocations and called for clear action plans with defined responsibilities. The concerned authorities were directed to submit actionable proposals within 15 days to address outstanding issues relating to the bypass project.

headline: Interior Minister oversees demolition of Khanna Police Station
description: ISLAMABAD - Federal Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Friday supervised the demolition of Khanna Police Station, built on the greenbelt along Islamabad
author: NEWS WIRE
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - Federal Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Friday supervised the demolition of Khanna Police Station, built on the greenbelt along Islamabad Expressway, as part of an operation against encroachments and illegal occupation of government land in the federal capital. The Chief Commissioner Islamabad and Inspector General of Islamabad Police also participated in the demolition operation. The Deputy Commissioner Islamabad and other concerned officials were present at the site.

Speaking during the operation, Mohsin Naqvi said Khanna Police Station had been temporarily shifted to an alternative location. He added that a new site had been legally allocated for the police station, where a new building would be constructed. The interior minister said no government or private organisation, or any individual, would be allowed to occupy government land. He added that land occupied by departments working under the Ministry of Interior was also being retrieved as part of the ongoing operation. Mohsin Naqvi reiterated that indiscriminate action against illegal occupation and encroachments would continue and that government land would be retrieved wherever it had been occupied.

headline: Building Control Directorate issues notice to Maulana Fazlur Rehman’s residence
description: ISLAMABAD - The Capital Development Authority (CDA) has issued a notice to the residence of Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman in
author: MUHAMMAD ASAD CHAUDHRY
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - The Capital Development Authority (CDA) has issued a notice to the residence of Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman in Islamabad, pointing out alleged violations of building regulations and directing the removal of the identified irregularities within 15 days.

According to the notice issued by the CDA’s Building Control Directorate, alleged unauthorised constructions have been identified within the setbacks of the residence, which are required to remain clear under the applicable building regulations. The authority has also raised objections to the installation of security guard posts and a generator on CDA-owned land, terming these installations violations requiring removal. The notice, issued by the Deputy Director Building Control, directed to remove all identified violations within 15 days of the issuance of the notice.

The CDA has warned that failure to comply with the directions within the stipulated period may lead to legal action under the relevant laws and regulations. It further cautioned that, in case of non-compliance, the building could be sealed and the alleged unauthorised structures demolished in accordance with the law.

However, the JUI-F has termed CDA’s action as a reactionary move and the son of Maulana Fazal-ur-Rehman in a social media post has questioned the issuance of said notice. Without naming anyone in his post, he said the whole system is being used to satisfy the ego and revenge of a person. On the other hand, when contacted, the building control officials claimed that the action is taken in routine after a survey of said house.

headline: Chairman CDA visits commercial centres; reviews development, renovation works
description: ISLAMABAD - In line with the vision of Federal Interior Minister Syed Mohsin Raza Naqvi and under the leadership of Chairman Capital Development Authority
author: PR
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - In line with the vision of Federal Interior Minister Syed Mohsin Raza Naqvi and under the leadership of Chairman Capital Development Authority (CDA) Sohail Ashraf, the Chairman CDA visited various commercial centres of Islamabad, including Kohsar Market, Jinnah Super Market (F-7) and F-6 Markaz, to review ongoing development, renovation and infrastructure improvement works.

During the visit, the Chairman CDA Sohail Ashraf reviewed the progress of ongoing upgradation, beautification and infrastructure improvement initiatives in different Marakiz. He was given a detailed briefing on the progress achieved so far, improvements in infrastructure, renovation of public spaces, and measures being undertaken to provide better facilities to citizens, shoppers and visitors to these Marakiz.

The Director General Infrastructure, Director General E&M, Chief Officer Metropolitan Corporation Islamabad (MCI), Deputy Commissioner Islamabad, Additional Deputy Commissioner (General), and the concerned Assistant Commissioner also accompanied the Chairman CDA during the visit. The relevant officers briefed him on ongoing development activities and the future course of action.

Chairman CDA Sohail Ashraf directed the concerned departments to further strengthen coordination and cooperation, expedite work wherever required, and ensure the timely completion of all development projects while maintaining construction quality and the highest standards of workmanship.

headline: Embassy of Russia hosts presentation of book ‘The Ukraine War: Beyond the Headlines’
description: ISLAMABAD - The discussion featured Ambassador Albert P. Khorev; Senator Mushahid Hussain Syed, former Chairman of the Senate Committees on Foreign Relations
author: Our Staff Reporter
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - The discussion featured Ambassador Albert P. Khorev; Senator Mushahid Hussain Syed, former Chairman of the Senate Committees on Foreign Relations and Defence; Ambassador Masood Khan, former Pakistani Ambassador to China and the U.S.; Lieutenant General (Retd.) Asad Durrani, former Director General of Inter-Services Intelligence; Dr. Almas Haider Naqvi, PhD Scholar at the School of Politics and International Relations, Quaid-i-Azam University; and Dr. Gul-i-Ayesha Bhatti, Assistant Professor at the School of Social Sciences and Humanities, National University of Sciences and Technology (NUST). The event also brought together prominent representatives of Pakistan’s academic community and media.

In his opening remarks, Ambassador Khorev thanked the author for his intellectual courage in seeking to document facts that challenge prevailing Western narratives. The Ambassador highlighted the book’s academic value, noting that it draws on official documents and data from the United Nations and other international organizations. Munir Ahmed’s work seeks to shed light on the underlying causes of the conflict in Ukraine, focusing on NATO’s eastward expansion in breach of commitments made in the 1990s, as well as the destructive policies of the Ukrainian and EU leadership that compelled Russia to launch the special military operation. “Consider the irony. Ukraine was meant to be a battering ram aimed at destroying Russia’s statehood. Instead, it has become a boomerang hitting Western economies,” he said.

Ambassador Khorev stressed that Russia’s objectives are not territorial in nature, but rather concern border security, the protection of Russian-speaking population and the fight against the spread of neo-Nazism. “Russia remains open to dialogue and peace. But peace must be based on justice, respect for the legitimate security interests of all parties and the recognition of the realities on the ground,” he noted. The Russian Ambassador focused on the damaging consequences of Western sanctions and efforts to target the so-called “shadow fleet” for global food and energy security. In closing, Ambassador Khorev expressed his gratitude to Pakistan’s leadership for maintaining a neutral position and reaffirmed Russia’s readiness to expand bilateral cooperation across all areas. In his remarks, Senator Mushahid Hussain Syed noted that developing relations with Russia is one of Pakistan’s key foreign policy priorities. He described NATO as a “relic of the past” and criticized the West’s policy of “demonizing” Russia, arguing that it had only contributed to the decline of the Western rules-based world order.

Ambassador Masood Khan praised Munir Ahmed’s work and called for an early end to the conflict. He emphasized the special responsibility of Russia and the United States for maintaining strategic stability and highlighted the considerable potential for Russia-Pakistan cooperation in the economic and humanitarian spheres.

Lieutenant General (Retd.) Asad Durrani outlined the historical context of Russia’s relations with Western countries, noting that NATO’s gradual eastward expansion had prompted Russia to take active countermeasures. Dr. Almas Haider Naqvi drew attention to biased and one-sided coverage of the Ukraine conflict in Western media, pointing to the use of Ukraine as an instrument to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia.

Dr. Gul-i-Ayesha Bhatti highlighted the shortage of English-language academic materials presenting Russia’s perspective on key international issues. She noted that Munir Ahmed’s book seeks to offer a more comprehensive picture of events, rather than reducing the conflict to “a simple story with a single villain.” Munir Ahmed’s book will soon be available in bookstores across Pakistan. It can also be purchased online through Amazon.

headline: 10 DSPs of Islamabad Police promoted to SP rank
description: ISLAMABAD - The Departmental Promotion Committee (DPC) has recommended promotion of 10 DSPs (BS-17) of Islamabad Police to the rank of SP (BS-18). The
author: Tahir Niaz
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - The Departmental Promotion Committee (DPC) has recommended promotion of 10 DSPs (BS-17) of Islamabad Police to the rank of SP (BS-18). The promotion will take effect immediately, and the promoted officers will remain on probation for one year. “Consequent upon the recommendations of Departmental Promotion Committee and subsequent approval by the competent authority i.e. Secretary Interior and Narcotics Control, following DSPs (BS-17) of ICT Police are promoted to the rank of Superintendents of Police (BS-18) in Islamabad Capital Territory Police with immediate effect,” read a notification issued by the Ministry of Interior on October 30. The promoted police officers are Tariq Mehmood, Khalid Mehmood Awan, Irshad Ali Abro, Sajid Abbas, Basharat Ali, Muhammad Sarfaraz, Fayyaz Ahmed, Asad Ullah Mangi, Akram Ali Soomro and Saat Ali Abro.

Separately, the government has ordered the deployment of 21 officers and employees to provide health facilities to inmates at the newly-constructed Islamabad Model Jail. The officers and employees belong to Capital Hospital Islamabad. All officers and employees have been placed on attachment with the approval of the Chief Commissioner and Chairman CDA. The services of the officers and employees have been handed over for the future at the request of the SSP of federal prisoners. All officers and employees have been directed to report immediately. The Islamabad jail is likely to be inaugurated within a few days and prisoners from Aidala jail in Rawalpindi would be shifted there.

headline: NSU hosts first Hepatitis C screening camp under Prime Minister’s national programme
description: ISLAMABAD - National Skills University (NSU), Islamabad, hosted the first Hepatitis C screening camp in federal universities under the Prime Minister’s
author: Our Staff Reporter
article_text:
ISLAMABAD - National Skills University (NSU), Islamabad, hosted the first Hepatitis C screening camp in federal universities under the Prime Minister’s National Hepatitis C Elimination Programme, marking an important step towards promoting preventive healthcare and public health awareness among the university community.

Chairman Higher Education Commission (HEC), Pakistan, Engr. Prof. Dr. Niaz Ahmad Akhtar, graced the inaugural ceremony as chief guest and formally inaugurated the screening camp at the university. The initiative was organized under the leadership and guidance of Prof. Dr. Saud Altaf, Vice Chancellor, National Skills University Islamabad, reflecting the university’s commitment to promoting health awareness, disease prevention and community welfare alongside academic and professional education.

The Department of Health Sciences Technology, headed by its Chairperson, Prof. Dr. M. Arif Nadeem Saqib, played a key role in coordinating and facilitating the screening activities. The camp offered Hepatitis C screening and diagnostic testing, medical counselling, referral services and access to treatment for eligible individuals. The initiative forms part of the national efforts to eliminate Hepatitis C from Pakistan by 2030 through early detection, timely treatment and increased public awareness.

The event highlighted the importance of collaboration among the Government of Pakistan, the Higher Education Commission and higher education institutions in addressing public health challenges. Through such initiatives, National Skills University Islamabad continues to contribute to national development by extending its role beyond education to community health and social responsibility

headline: CM Murad invites Portuguese firms to invest in Karachi’s water desalination, energy sector
description: KARACHI - Sindh Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah, in his meeting with Portugal’s Ambassador to Pakistan, Mr Paulo Domingues, invited Portuguese
author: Our Staff Reporter
article_text:
KARACHI - Sindh Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah, in his meeting with Portugal’s Ambassador to Pakistan, Mr Paulo Domingues, invited Portuguese companies to partner with the Sindh government in addressing Karachi’s growing water requirements through modern desalination technology, while also exploring investment opportunities in the energy sector and cooperation in football development. He proposed linking Portuguese companies with the Karachi Water and Sewerage Corporation (KWSC) to jointly examine the technical and commercial feasibility of establishing desalination plants in Karachi.

Portugal’s Political Officer David Arcaú, Honorary Consul of Portugal in Karachi Amin Fakar, and Secre-tary to the Chief Minister Asif Jameel attended the meeting at CM House. During the meeting, the two sides discussed opportunities to strengthen bilateral cooperation in water resources, energy, sports, particularly football, and investment. Welcoming the Portuguese Ambassador, CM Murad Ali Shah said the Sindh government was actively exploring sustainable solutions to meet Karachi’s increasing water demand, and desalination was an important option being considered. “We want to benefit from modern technology and international expertise to ensure the provision of clean drinking water to the people of Karachi and address the province’s energy challenges,” the Chief Minister said.

He proposed that Portuguese companies with expertise in desalination technology be connected with the Karachi Water and Sewerage Corporation to explore the possibility of establishing desalination plants in the city. Murad Shah said Portuguese companies and KWSC could jointly assess the technical requirements, available technologies, investment models and feasibility of potential projects. “Portugal has valuable technological expertise in water management and desalination. We want to benefit from this experi-ence to develop sustainable and modern water supply solutions for Karachi,” the Chief Minister said. He added that the provincial government was keen to encourage international partnerships that could introduce innovative technologies, improve service delivery and strengthen Karachi’s water infrastruc-ture.

The Chief Minister also discussed opportunities for Portuguese investment in Sindh’s energy sector, particularly through modern technology, technical cooperation and private-sector partnerships. He directed the Investment Department to establish contact with the Portuguese Embassy and ex-plore potential areas of investment and cooperation with Portuguese companies. CM Murad Ali Shah said Sindh was open to international investment and technological partnerships that could contribute to energy security, infrastructure development and sustainable economic growth. The two sides agreed to maintain close coordination to identify viable projects and translate the dis-cussions into practical cooperation.

Discussing sports cooperation, the Chief Minister highlighted Lyari’s rich footballing culture and said the area had considerable talent among its young footballers. He stressed the need to provide young players with international-standard training, professional coaching and opportunities to develop their skills. “Lyari has tremendous footballing talent. We want our young players to benefit from Portugal’s rich footballing experience, modern coaching techniques and international standards of training,” he said.

The meeting discussed opportunities for Portuguese football institutions, coaches and sports organisa-tions to collaborate with local institutions in Sindh to promote grassroots football and develop young talent. Both sides agreed to explore practical arrangements for training programmes, coaching exchanges and exposure opportunities for promising young footballers from Lyari.

Ambassador Paulo Domingues expressed keen interest in strengthening Portugal’s cooperation with Sindh in different sectors, particularly water management, desalination, energy and sports. He showed interest in exploring opportunities for Portuguese companies to share their technological expertise and participate in potential projects in Karachi and other parts of Sindh. The Ambassador also welcomed the proposal to establish direct engagement between Portuguese companies and KWSC to examine desalination opportunities.

headline: Court hands down death sentence to 5 brothers for committing triple murder
description: Rawalpindi - An additional district and sessions judge (ADSJ) on Friday handed down death sentence to five brothers for stabbing three
author: OUR STAFF REPORT
article_text:
Rawalpindi - An additional district and sessions judge (ADSJ) on Friday handed down death sentence to five brothers for stabbing three persons – a couple and their son – for honour in the limits of Kallar Syedan police in 2023. ADSJ Jehangir Ali Gondal convicted Kashif, Ahsan, Asif, Ismail, and Yasir, sons of Wazir Butt and residents of Dhoke Fazal Din and sentenced them to death for killing Muhammad Shabir, his wife Rukhsana Begum, and their son Muhammad Saghir in Dhoke Baba Fazal Din Dhakhli Mak Phalina Road in Kallar Syedan on July 18, 2023. The court directed each of the five convicts to pay Rs 200,000 to every legal heir of the three murdered persons. In case of default, each convict had to undergo six months jail and the compensation money would be deducted as arrears of land revenue. In addition to the capital punishment, the court sentenced each convict to five years of rigorous imprisonment for house trespass under section 452 of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC) and a fine of Rs 20,000. They were also sentenced to two years of jail for rioting armed with deadly weapons under section 148 PPC along with a fine of Rs 5,000 each.

Muhammad Saleem Akhtar, brother of deceased Rukhsana Begum, lodged the FIR with Kallar Syedan police saying the five brothers with their father and two unknown men entered the house of Muhammad Shabir forcibly and attacked Shabir, his wife and son with knives and killed Saghir and Rukhsana at the spot while Shabir died later in the hospital.

The complainant said that the reason behind the murder was honor as the killers suspected Muhammad Idress, son of deceased Shabir, had illicit relations with wife of convict Yasir. They committed the murder as they had grudge against Idrees and his family.

headline: Dearth of sludge suits risks health of rescuers
description: Rawalpindi - Shortage of protective sludge suits for staff of Rescue 1122 in Rawalpindi has been a cause of concern among the rescuers who often
author: OUR STAFF REPORT
article_text:
Rawalpindi - Shortage of protective sludge suits for staff of Rescue 1122 in Rawalpindi has been a cause of concern among the rescuers who often have to wade through slush and muddy waters of drains and nullah in search of drowned persons.

During background discussions with numerous rescuers, The Nation has learnt that more often than not the rescuers involved in body search in the dangerously hazardous waters of the city drains and nullahs that had been receiving untreated sewerage water. The rescuers complained that they had to wade through the wastewater for hours for search of dead bodies after people drown or children swept away during monsoon rains.

Many rescuers who spoke on condition of anonymity said that they had to follow the orders and had to do the work as very basic human job. They often do not get personal protective equipment (PPE) such as sludge suits when they enter the water and spend hours inside the hazardous chemical filled water.

An experienced rescuers who had been with the force for a long time in the garrison city said that many of the boys get itching and rashes on their bodies after they enter the slush without protective gear. headline: Punjab government targets 1.6m acres in Rawalpindi division for wheat cultivation
description: Rawalpindi - Punjab Minister for Agriculture Syed Ashiq Hussain Kirmani and Secretary Agriculture Punjab Shakeel Ahmad Mian paid an official visit
author: OUR STAFF REPORT
article_text:
Rawalpindi - Punjab Minister for Agriculture Syed Ashiq Hussain Kirmani and Secretary Agriculture Punjab Shakeel Ahmad Mian paid an official visit to Rawalpindi on Friday to review measures for boosting wheat cultivation across the region.

Presiding over a high-level meeting at the commissioner office Rawalpindi, Minister Kirmani announced that the provincial government has set a proposed wheat price of Rs 4,500 per maund to encourage local farmers. A total cultivation target of 16.5 million acres has been fixed for Punjab during the current season, including 1.6 million acres dedicated to the Rawalpindi division.

The minister stated that special tasks have been assigned to field formations to ensure wheat cultivation exceeds the established targets. Emphasizing that wheat remains vital for national food security, he noted that key government initiatives have transformed its cultivation into a profitable enterprise for growers.

To boost the adoption of certified seed varieties, the provincial government is providing a Rs320 million in subsidy, making Punjab Seed Corporation’s certified wheat seed available to farmers at Rs 7,000 per bag after an Rs 800 subsidy. Furthermore, Rs17 billion in interest-free loans is being allocated for DAP fertilizer purchases covering 5 million acres. Under the Kisan Card initiative, approximately one million farmers will receive an additional interest-free loan of Rs 3,500 per acre.

Secretary Agriculture Shakeel Ahmad Mian informed the meeting that the Agriculture Transformation Plan is being actively executed across the Potohar region, supported by continuous field monitoring. He highlighted the essential role of divisional and district administrations in reaching the province’s target goals.

The meeting was attended by Parliamentary Secretary for Zakat & Ushr Malik Iftikhar Ahmad MPA, Malik Itbar Khan MPA, deputy commissioners from across the Rawalpindi division, Agriculture Department directors general, relevant officers, local farmers, and other key stakeholders.

headline: Past in Perspective
description: The Arab Spring, which began in late 2010, was a series of pro-democracy uprisings and protests across several Arab countries, including Tunisia, Egypt, Libya,
author: The Nation
article_text: The Arab Spring, which began in late 2010, was a series of pro-democracy uprisings and protests across several Arab countries, including Tunisia, Egypt, Libya, Syria, and Bahrain. Sparked by discontent with authoritarian rule, corruption, and socioeconomic inequality, these movements aimed to bring about political reform, social justice, and greater freedoms. The Arab Spring’s significance lies in its role in toppling entrenched regimes, inspiring hope for democratic change, and highlighting the power of grassroots activism and social media in mobilising populations. Though outcomes varied across countries, the Arab Spring continues to influence political discourse, activism, and governance in the region today.

headline: Role of Technology in Healthcare
description: Healthcare is essential to a country’s social and economic development. In Pakistan, however, access to quality healthcare remains a major challenge,
author: The Nation
article_text:
Healthcare is essential to a country’s social and economic development. In Pakistan, however, access to quality healthcare remains a major challenge, particularly in rural and underserved areas where qualified doctors, well-equipped hospitals, and affordable treatment are often difficult to access. Technology can help address these gaps by making healthcare more accessible, efficient, and affordable.

Telemedicine is one of the most practical applications of technology. Through video calls, phone consultations, and digital platforms, patients can consult doctors without travelling long distances. Initiatives such as Sehat Kahani demonstrate how digital healthcare can connect patients with medical professionals, particularly in underserved communities. Telemedicine can also reduce travel costs and simplify follow-up care for patients with chronic illnesses.

Technology can improve mental healthcare as well. Online counselling and telepsychiatry offer additional ways for people to seek support, especially where mental health professionals are scarce or stigma discourages in-person visits. However, online services should complement face-to-face treatment when physical assessment or emergency intervention is necessary.

Digital health records can help doctors access patients’ medical histories, prescriptions, and test results more efficiently. They can reduce the risk of lost information and improve coordination between hospitals, clinics, and laboratories. Similarly, artificial intelligence (AI) can assist in analysing medical scans, identifying disease patterns, and supporting clinical decisions. However, AI should complement, not replace, medical professionals and their judgement.

Pakistan’s widespread mobile phone use also creates opportunities for health awareness. Mobile applications, SMS alerts, and digital campaigns can provide information about vaccination, nutrition, maternal health, hygiene, and disease prevention. Digital systems can also strengthen public health monitoring and improve communication during disease outbreaks and emergencies.

Technology could help narrow the healthcare gap between urban and rural communities. Rural health workers equipped with digital devices could consult specialists in major cities, while patients could receive medical advice without travelling long distances. However, unreliable internet connectivity, limited electricity, and the cost of digital services remain significant barriers.

Other concerns include patient privacy, data security, and digital literacy. Medical information must be protected, and both healthcare professionals and patients need training to use digital systems effectively. Moreover, online consultations cannot replace every physical examination, diagnostic test, or emergency procedure.

To maximise technology’s benefits, Pakistan must invest in reliable internet infrastructure, train healthcare professionals, strengthen data protection, and establish clear standards for digital healthcare services. Government institutions, hospitals, universities, and technology companies must also collaborate to develop solutions that meet patients’ needs.

Technology is already becoming an important part of healthcare. Telemedicine can connect patients with doctors, digital records can improve information management, AI can support diagnosis, and mobile platforms can spread health awareness. However, these benefits will remain limited unless affordability, accessibility, and patient safety are prioritised.

The goal should not simply be to digitise healthcare, but to make it more accessible, affordable, efficient, and humane. With careful planning and a commitment to equal access, technology can help improve the health and lives of millions of people across Pakistan.

ALISHBA ASLAM,

Karachi.

headline: The Charms of Youth
description: Youth is a special stage of life, marked by energy, curiosity and opportunity. With proper care, confidence and a positive outlook, young people can contribute
author: The Nation
article_text:
Youth is a special stage of life, marked by energy, curiosity and opportunity. With proper care, confidence and a positive outlook, young people can contribute greatly to society.

However, many waste valuable time on social media instead of developing skills, reading or concentrating on their education. Excessive screen time can prevent them from discovering their talents and pursuing their ambitions.

Another concern is the difficulty some young people face in dealing with criticism and setbacks. Even minor disappointments can undermine their confidence and discourage them from moving forward. Learning to handle challenges constructively is an essential part of personal growth.

Families, schools and communities can help young people make better use of their time by providing mentorship, safe spaces to discuss their concerns, and opportunities to participate in sports, creative activities and community projects. Education should also encourage practical skills such as public speaking, problem-solving and creative writing.

Young people need guidance, encouragement and emotional resilience to navigate life’s challenges. By reducing distractions and making the most of their abilities, they can turn the opportunities of youth into lasting achievements.

IRUM GHULAM MUSTAFA,

Hub.

headline: Private School Fees
description: I wish to draw attention to the growing burden of private school fees on ordinary families. Education is a fundamental right, and parents naturally want
author: The Nation
article_text:
I wish to draw attention to the growing burden of private school fees on ordinary families. Education is a fundamental right, and parents naturally want to provide their children with quality schooling. However, rising tuition fees and additional charges are making this increasingly difficult.

Admission fees, examination charges, books, uniforms, transport and other expenses add considerably to the cost of education. Families on limited incomes are often forced to make difficult choices between their children’s schooling and other essential household needs.

Private schools play an important role in providing educational opportunities, but their fee structures should reflect parents’ financial circumstances. I urge school administrations to keep fees reasonable, avoid unnecessary charges and carefully consider the impact of increases on families.

Education should be an investment in the future, not an unbearable financial burden. I hope school administrations will take practical steps to make quality education more affordable.

BANADI WAHID,

Kech.

headline: Pakistan’s Diplomatic Renaissance
description: In global politics, a country’s strategic influence is evaluated not only by its military strength or economic profile but also by its diplomatic ability
author: Zaid Bin Inam
article_text:
In global politics, a country’s strategic influence is evaluated not only by its military strength or economic profile but also by its diplomatic ability to shape conversations, facilitate the process of negotiations, and prevent conflicts from spiralling out of proportion. Pakistan’s diplomatic engagement following the Iran-Israel conflict has brought this dimension of national power into sharper focus. At a time when the Middle East has become an arena of power contestation and strategic uncertainty, Islamabad has sought to reposition itself as a voice for de-escalation of conflict and act as a potential bridge between the competing powers. The important question is whether this diplomatic prominence can be transformed into a sustainable global profile.

Pakistan’s engagement with the crisis reflects a combination of strategic relationships, geography, and diplomatic necessity. Sharing a border with Iran while maintaining longstanding security and economic ties with Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states, Pakistan has direct interests in the stability of the Middle East. Consequently, diplomacy is not simply an expression of goodwill; it is an essential instrument for protecting Pakistan’s national interest.

The escalation of hostilities involving Israel, Iran and the United States in 2026 created a challenging environment for Islamabad. Pakistan had to strategically navigate the competing relationships without becoming entangled in a wider regional confrontation. Its response centred on calls for restraint, respect for international law and the restoration of dialogue. Pakistan also sought to maintain communication with Washington and Tehran while coordinating with regional partners. These efforts have helped bring Islamabad greater visibility in discussions concerning regional peace and security. The significance of this diplomatic engagement at the regional and international level lies in Pakistan’s attempt to move beyond issuing statements of concern towards facilitating communication between parties that have limited trust in one another. In April 2026, Pakistan hosted direct US-Iran talks, and subsequent negotiations produced an Islamabad memorandum of understanding in June. The diplomatic process demonstrated that Islamabad could provide a channel for negotiations even when the prospect for a durable settlement remained uncertain. This distinction matters. A successful diplomatic initiative is not necessarily one that immediately ends a conflict. It can also involve keeping communication channels open, reducing the risk of miscalculations, and creating opportunities for renewed negotiations. Pakistan’s diplomatic credibility will ultimately depend on whether its efforts produce tangible and sustainable outcomes.

Pakistan’s contemporary diplomatic profile is closely connected to its geographical position. Situated at the intersection of South Asia, Central Asia and the Middle East, the country occupies a strategic space linking major regional and middle powers, energy corridors and geo-strategic flashpoints. Its proximity to Iran, access to the Arabian Sea, and relationship with Gulf countries provide Islamabad with opportunities to participate in discussions extending beyond its immediate neighbourhood. Geography alone does not generate influence. It becomes strategically valuable when supported by effective diplomacy, reliable partnerships, and the capacity to deliver results. Pakistan’s engagement with the Israel-Iran crisis illustrates how geographical proximity can become a diplomatic asset when a country maintains working relationships with opposing sides. The same logic applies to Pakistan’s relations with China and the US. Islamabad’s longstanding partnership with Beijing and its renewed engagement with Washington offer opportunities to diversify its diplomatic portfolio. Rather than presenting these relationships as competing choices, Pakistan can seek cooperation with both powers on issues where their interests overlap, including regional stability, counter-terrorism, and economic connectivity.

Pakistan’s diplomatic engagement also reflects an effort to broaden its international identity. For years, external perceptions of the country have often been dominated by security concerns, political instability, and economic vulnerability. Its recent mediation initiatives offer an opportunity to demonstrate a different dimension of national capacity: the national ability to convene, communicate, and facilitate confidence-building measures. This diplomatic opportunity suggests that a country with constrained economic resources can still exercise diplomatic influence when circumstances align with its strategic relationships and institutional capabilities. Pakistan’s regional coordination with Türkiye and Saudi Arabia through the trilateral Makkah Defence Agreement may create additional avenues for consultation on Middle Eastern security. The Badr agreement, officially known as the Badr Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), is a four-country defence cooperation agreement signed by Pakistan, Türkiye, Qatar, and Indonesia on 21 October 2026 in Doha, Qatar. This agreement is important for Pakistan in the realm of defence self-reliance, access to technology, and wider strategic partnerships.

Diplomatic recognition cannot compensate indefinitely for domestic weaknesses. Pakistan continues to face economic constraints, external financing pressures, security challenges, and political uncertainty. These factors affect its capacity to sustain international initiatives and limit the resources available for long-term diplomatic engagement. Moreover, Washington and Tehran have their own strategic calculations, domestic pressures, and security objectives.

Pakistan now faces a critical choice: treat its diplomatic visibility as a temporary achievement or use it as the foundation for a more coherent international strategy. The latter requires strengthening economic diplomacy, attracting investment, improving regional connectivity, and developing expertise in conflict mediation. It requires greater coordination between diplomatic institutions, economic policymakers, and security decision-makers.

The Israel-Iran conflict has demonstrated that Pakistan can find diplomatic space even amid intense geopolitical competition. Its relationship with Washington, Tehran, Beijing, and the Gulf capitals creates opportunities, but they also impose demanding balancing requirements. Pakistan’s diplomatic engagement is an opening that could help the country redefine aspects of its international profile. In a world increasingly shaped by confrontation, the ability to bring adversaries to the negotiating table remains a valuable form of national power.

Zaid Bin Inam The writer is an academician and faculty member at NUML.

At a time when the Middle East has become an arena of power contestation and strategic uncertainty, Islamabad has sought to reposition itself as a voice for de-escalation of conflict and act as a potential bridge between the competing powers. The important question is whether this diplomatic prominence can be transformed into a sustainable global profile.

content_blocks.text: The escalation of hostilities involving Israel, Iran and the United States in 2026 created a challenging environment for Islamabad. Pakistan had to strategically navigate the competing relationships without becoming entangled in a wider regional confrontation. Its response centred on calls for restraint, respect for international law and the restoration of dialogue. Pakistan also sought to maintain communication with Washington and Tehran while coordinating with regional partners. These efforts have helped bring Islamabad greater visibility in discussions concerning regional peace and security. The significance of this diplomatic engagement at the regional and international level lies in Pakistan’s attempt to move beyond issuing statements of concern towards facilitating communication between parties that have limited trust in one another. In April 2026, Pakistan hosted direct US-Iran talks, and subsequent negotiations produced an Islamabad memorandum of understanding in June. The diplomatic process demonstrated that Islamabad could provide a channel for negotiations even when the prospect for a durable settlement remained uncertain. This distinction matters. A successful diplomatic initiative is not necessarily one that immediately ends a conflict. It can also involve keeping communication channels open, reducing the risk of miscalculations, and creating opportunities for renewed negotiations. Pakistan’s diplomatic credibility will ultimately depend on whether its efforts produce tangible and sustainable outcomes.

content_blocks.text: Pakistan’s contemporary diplomatic profile is closely connected to its geographical position. Situated at the intersection of South Asia, Central Asia and the Middle East, the country occupies a strategic space linking major regional and middle powers, energy corridors and geo-strategic flashpoints. Its proximity to Iran, access to the Arabian Sea, and relationship with Gulf countries provide Islamabad with opportunities to participate in discussions extending beyond its immediate neighbourhood. Geography alone does not generate influence. It becomes strategically valuable when supported by effective diplomacy, reliable partnerships, and the capacity to deliver results. Pakistan’s engagement with the Israel-Iran crisis illustrates how geographical proximity can become a diplomatic asset when a country maintains working relationships with opposing sides. The same logic applies to Pakistan’s relations with China and the US. Islamabad’s longstanding partnership with Beijing and its renewed engagement with Washington offer opportunities to diversify its diplomatic portfolio. Rather than presenting these relationships as competing choices, Pakistan can seek cooperation with both powers on issues where their interests overlap, including regional stability, counter-terrorism, and economic connectivity.

headline: Educated But Uncivil

author: Muhammad Awais
article_text:
At a red light on any main road in Lahore this week, watch the tinted window of an expensive vehicle come down. A coffee cup, a wrapper, and a tissue land on the road. The window closes. The light turns green.

The man behind that glass is educated. He is prosperous. He is very likely on his way to an office where he will complain, with real feeling, about the state of this country.

We spend our days blaming institutions for our decline. This particular failure requires no institution at all. It requires only a citizen who has decided that nothing outside his own four walls belongs to him.

Begin with the roads, because that is where the disease is most visible. Signals treated as suggestions. Wrong-side driving as a routine shortcut. Hospital entrances blocked by parked vehicles while an ambulance waits behind them. Footpaths, built at public expense for people who cannot afford cars, occupied by the cars of people who can.

Confront any of it, and you will rarely hear an apology. You will hear a name. A rank, a relative, a party, a designation. VIP culture in Pakistan is no longer confined to protocol convoys and police outriders. It has been democratised. Anyone with a plate, a badge, or a cousin now carries a small portable version of it.

Then there is the paradox that should shame us most. Homes scrubbed to a shine. Cars vacuumed weekly. And the moment the boundary of private property is crossed, the entire country becomes a bin.

The Margalla trails are strewn with plastic bottles left there by the same families who drove up to enjoy the view. Beaches, parks, upmarket markets, the courtyards of shrines: all of it decorated with the litter of the classes who use them. This is not a poverty problem. The poor do not generate imported snack packaging.

Jane Jacobs wrote in The Death and Life of Great American Cities that “cities have the capability of providing something for everybody.” She added the condition that we keep failing to meet: only when they are created by everybody.

A nation is not what it builds inside its walls. It is what it leaves on the other side of them.

The wealthier neighbourhoods have gone further and simply annexed the commons. Gates, cones and barriers appear across public streets in housing societies, with private guards deciding who may drive down a road that every taxpayer helped to lay. Residents call it security. In law it is encroachment, and it is done openly, because nobody expects consequences.

Zoning has collapsed in the same way. Purely residential streets now host schools, boutiques, salons and cafés, each generating traffic and noise that the neighbours never agreed to absorb. The by-laws exist. They are simply priced into the cost of doing business.

The smaller cruelties tell the same story. The man who walks past forty people at an airport counter because queuing is beneath him. The horn pressed continuously outside a hospital ward. The wedding sound system at two in the morning in a street with newborn children and night-shift workers in it.

None of this is ignorance. Everyone in these examples can read a sign. They have decided the sign is for someone else.

Now the same conduct has moved online, where it has found no friction at all. Educated professionals forward unverified claims to family groups within seconds of receiving them. Strangers are filmed without consent so they can be mocked to an audience of thousands. Addresses are published, women are hounded, and the pile-on is defended as opinion. The mob did not disappear. It acquired a data plan.

Robert Putnam identified the missing element in Bowling Alone: “the norms of reciprocity and trustworthiness that arise from them.” Networks alone are not community. What binds a society is the assumption that other people’s lives carry weight equal to your own. That assumption is now visibly absent from our public conduct, and no literacy rate compensates for it.

Repair is possible, but it will not come from another awareness campaign. Enforcement must stop at nobody’s nameplate; a points-based licensing system with published violation records would do more than a thousand billboards. Municipal fines for littering and encroachment must actually be collected, with camera enforcement in the major cities and the proceeds visibly spent on the same streets. Removal of illegal barriers and commercial encroachment should be a measurable duty of mayors and administrators, published quarterly. Civic conduct belongs in schools as daily practice rather than a chapter in a textbook. And the first prosecutions must be of the powerful, because in this country deterrence has only ever travelled downwards from the top.

The urgency is not aesthetic. A society that will not respect a queue, a footpath or a neighbour’s sleep has stopped believing in the idea that holds it together.

A country that cannot be trusted with its own footpaths will not be trusted with its future.

Long Live Pakistan!

Muhammad Awais The writer is an engineer. He can be reached at: gcawais91@gmail.com

article_html:
At a red light on any main road in Lahore this week, watch the tinted window of an expensive vehicle come down. A coffee cup, a wrapper, and a tissue land on the road. The window closes. The light turns green.

The man behind that glass is educated. He is prosperous. He is very likely on his way to an office where he will complain, with real feeling, about the state of this country.

We spend our days blaming institutions for our decline. This particular failure requires no institution at all. It requires only a citizen who has decided that nothing outside his own four walls belongs to him.

Federal Constitutional Court upholds finality of judgments, rejects repeated challenges in land dispute

Begin with the roads, because that is where the disease is most visible. Signals treated as suggestions. Wrong-side driving as a routine shortcut. Hospital entrances blocked by parked vehicles while an ambulance waits behind them. Footpaths, built at public expense for people who cannot afford cars, occupied by the cars of people who can.

Confront any of it, and you will rarely hear an apology. You will hear a name. A rank, a relative, a party, a designation. VIP culture in Pakistan is no longer confined to protocol convoys and police outriders. It has been democratised. Anyone with a plate, a badge, or a cousin now carries a small portable version of it.

DG ISPR says Pakistan-Saudi defence cooperation could expand, rules out wider military campaigns

Then there is the paradox that should shame us most. Homes scrubbed to a shine. Cars vacuumed weekly. And the moment the boundary of private property is crossed, the entire 
country becomes a bin.

The Margalla trails are strewn with plastic bottles left there by the same families who drove up to enjoy the view. Beaches, parks, upmarket markets, the courtyards of shrines: all of it decorated with the litter of the classes who use them. This is not a poverty problem. The poor do not generate imported snack packaging.

Qatar offers Pakistani travellers free 30-day visa on arrival under four conditions

Jane Jacobs wrote in The Death and Life of Great American Cities that “cities have the capability of providing something for everybody.” She added the condition that we keep failing to meet: only when they are created by everybody.

A nation is not what it builds inside its walls. It is what it leaves on the other side of them.

The wealthier neighbourhoods have gone further and simply annexed the commons. Gates, cones and barriers appear across public streets in housing societies, with private guards deciding who may drive down a road that every taxpayer helped to lay. Residents call it security. In law it is encroachment, and it is done openly, because nobody expects consequences.

ECP targets registration of 174,845 women voters in two-district pilot project

Zoning has collapsed in the same way. Purely residential streets now host schools, boutiques, salons and cafés, each generating traffic and noise that the neighbours never agreed to absorb. The by-laws exist. They are simply priced into the cost of doing business.

The smaller cruelties tell the same story. The man who walks past forty people at an airport counter because queuing is beneath him. The horn pressed continuously outside a hospital ward. The wedding sound system at two in the morning in a street with newborn children and night-shift workers in it.

APHC leader links Indian policies in Kashmir with Israeli practices in Palestine

None of this is ignorance. Everyone in these examples can read a sign. They have decided the sign is for someone else.

Now the same conduct has moved online, where it has found no friction at all. Educated professionals forward unverified claims to family groups within seconds of receiving them. Strangers are filmed without consent so they can be mocked to an audience of thousands. Addresses are published, women are hounded, and the pile-on is defended as opinion. The mob did not disappear. It acquired a data plan.

Robert Putnam identified the missing element in Bowling Alone: “the norms of reciprocity and trustworthiness that arise from them.” Networks alone are not community. What binds a society is the assumption that other people’s lives carry weight equal to your own. That assumption is now visibly absent from our public conduct, and no literacy rate compensates for it.

Repair is possible, but it will not come from another awareness campaign. Enforcement must stop at nobody’s nameplate; a points-based licensing system with published violation records would do more than a thousand billboards. Municipal fines for littering and encroachment must actually be collected, with camera enforcement in the major cities and the proceeds visibly spent on the same streets. Removal of illegal barriers and commercial encroachment should be a measurable duty of mayors and administrators, published quarterly. Civic conduct belongs in schools as daily practice rather than a chapter in a textbook. And the first prosecutions must be of the powerful, because in this country deterrence has only ever travelled downwards from the top.

The urgency is not aesthetic. A society that will not respect a queue, a footpath or a neighbour’s sleep has stopped believing in the idea that holds it together.

A country that cannot be trusted with its own footpaths will not be trusted with its future.

Long Live Pakistan!

Muhammad Awais
The writer is an engineer. He can be reached at: gcawais91@gmail.com

headline: Golden Handcuffs
description: The October sun in Islamabad is a merciful dictator. It forces the city to slow under its golden gaze. At a corner table of a plush restaurant – the kind
author: Najm us Saqib
article_text:
The October sun in Islamabad is a merciful dictator. It forces the city to slow under its golden gaze. At a corner table of a plush restaurant – the kind where the décor screams of an era of opulence and the chandeliers are polished to a blinding shine – four retired Ambassadors settled into their chairs. The air was thick with the scent of jasmine and old-money privilege. It was a beautiful October afternoon, the sort that makes you forget the world’s troubles, until the conversation turns to the world you left behind.

First: I hear the new Foreign Secretary is already packing up. Due to hit sixty next month. The twenty-seventh, isn’t it?

Second: (with a wry smile) Ah, but you forget. He’s not packing up. He’s unpacking. Another two years, at least. They’ve prepared a contractual extension.

First: (sighing, a sound filled with decades of bureaucratic fatigue) Of course they have. Barely a month in the chair, and now a fresh lease on professional life, well past sixty. It’s the Civil Servants Act, 1973, all over again. The standard age is sixty. Extensions are supposed to be exceptions requiring special approval, public-interest justification, etc. We have a framework, but we treat it like a suggestion.

Third: Seems like a pattern. His predecessor retired on the seventeenth of September, and within a heartbeat, Ambassador to Türkiye on a contract. The rationale is always the same. Leadership continuity. Bypassing the limit, keeping the ship steady.

Fourth: It’s becoming standard procedure. We promote people at the very precipice of retirement, handing them a fresh lease on the pretext that the country is desperately short of talent. It’s a convenient fiction. And we rob the next in line of their dreams and opportunities. I have nothing against the individuals. In fact, some are as dear to me as younger siblings. My concern is the principle. If thirty-five years of service, in good health, at the peak of your abilities, haven’t been enough to make your contribution, what will another two years achieve? Osteoporosis, stents, and enlarged prostates included? Surely, it’s time we trusted the next generation.

Second: Look at India. Their Cabinet Secretary can serve for up to three years past sixty. Home, Defence, IB, CBI, RAW – two years, capped, explicit. Strictly regulated, never a matter of right. They cap it. We pretend there’s no ceiling at all.

Third: And yet, the choice of Foreign Secretary is the government’s prerogative. It’s a selection post. No argument about that. But are non-selectees nobody? We live in an era of retired rulers. Our society is still organised by the colonial model of rulers and the ruled. Naturally, one clings to the ruling class as long as possible. I wouldn’t be surprised if bankers or businessmen were appointed Foreign Secretary tomorrow. Gosh.

First: Come to think of it, even if, by a stroke of a miracle, our colonial mindset were to change, there would still be those who want more for themselves. Greed is natural. But one must keep it in check to be able to face oneself at the end of the day. By the way, you didn’t cling. You turned down your extension.

Third: I did. And I’ve regretted it every Tuesday since.

Fourth: Experience suggests that people seldom turn down such opportunities if offered. It is human nature. Sixty is too young to retire. Fine. No harm if it’s applied across the board. For our people, even seventy will be too young. Why compensate selectively? It’s a small price for retaining the best while the rest wait their turn.

Second: That’s the argument, is it?

Fourth: It is an argument. When a true social contract evolves, and being a law-abiding citizen is enough to get by, there will be less incentive to extend one’s public-office status.

The Third looked out at the manicured lawns and said: You’ve put things in perspective.

Second: I usually do. That’s why they kept me on. (laughing at his own joke, then stopping quite suddenly).

Third: The deeper truth is that many civil servants resist retirement because it strips them of the only identity they have learned to value. However, the same officers who call their own extension indispensable call a colleague’s extension a self-serving obstruction. They do not oppose extensions. They oppose extensions that are not their own. In the end, the cribbing is not about rules or merit. It is the bruised vanity of people who want the door held open for themselves while demanding it be shut on everyone else.

Second: (quietly, for once not performing) Continuity isn’t nothing, you know. Ask anyone who’s watched a green Foreign Secretary get rolled by a counterpart who’s been in the room since the last century. The relationships take decades. That’s the argument they make. It’s not always a lie.

Third: No. It isn’t. But it’s never the whole truth either.

First: (raising his glass) To the next generation. May they live long enough to be extended.

(The table laughed. It was the kind of laugh that usually ends too soon.)

The clink of fine china and the distant hum of the city were the only sounds. It was a beautiful afternoon, but the shadow of the inevitable – retirement, the extension, the cycle – hung over the table, as heavy as the October sun. The question of who truly benefits from this perpetual lease on power, and who is left waiting in the wings, remained unanswered. The First and the Third, both of whom had once said no to an extension, one of them twice, sat in the shade of that question and did not care to look at it directly. The sun moved an inch across the lawn. Neither of them moved at all.

Najm us Saqib The writer is a former Ambassador of Pakistan and author of eight books in three languages. He can be reached at najmussaqib1960@msn.com

article_html:
The October sun in Islamabad is a merciful dictator. It forces the city to slow under its golden gaze. At a corner table of a plush restaurant – the kind where the décor screams of an era of opulence and the chandeliers are polished to a blinding shine – four retired Ambassadors settled into their chairs. The air was thick with the scent of jasmine and old-money privilege. It was a beautiful October afternoon, the sort that makes you forget the world’s troubles, until the conversation turns to the world you left behind.

First: I hear the new Foreign Secretary is already packing up. Due to hit sixty next month. The twenty-seventh, isn’t it?

Federal Constitutional Court upholds finality of judgments, rejects repeated challenges in land dispute

Second: (with a wry smile) Ah, but you forget. He’s not packing up. He’s unpacking. Another two years, at least. They’ve prepared a contractual extension.

First: (sighing, a sound filled with decades of bureaucratic fatigue) Of course they have. Barely a month in the chair, and now a fresh lease on professional life, well past sixty. It’s the Civil Servants Act, 1973, all over again. The standard age is sixty. Extensions are supposed to be exceptions requiring special approval, public-interest justification, etc. We have a framework, but we treat it like a suggestion.

DG ISPR says Pakistan-Saudi defence cooperation could expand, rules out wider military campaigns

Third: Seems like a pattern. His predecessor retired on the seventeenth of September, and within a heartbeat, Ambassador to Türkiye on a contract. The rationale is always the same. Leadership continuity. Bypassing the limit, keeping the ship steady.

Fourth: It’s becoming standard procedure. We promote people at the very precipice of retirement, handing them a fresh lease on the pretext that the country is desperately short of talent. It’s a convenient fiction. And we rob the next in line of their dreams and opportunities. I have nothing against the individuals. In fact, some are as dear to me as younger siblings. My concern is the principle. If thirty-five years of service, in good health, at the peak of your abilities, haven’t been enough to make your contribution, what will another two years achieve? Osteoporosis, stents, and enlarged prostates included? Surely, it’s time we trusted the next generation.

Qatar offers Pakistani travellers free 30-day visa on arrival under four conditions

Second: Look at India. Their Cabinet Secretary can serve for up to three years past sixty. Home, Defence, IB, CBI, RAW – two years, capped, explicit. Strictly regulated, never a matter of right. They cap it. We pretend there’s no ceiling at all.

Third: And yet, the choice of Foreign Secretary is the government’s prerogative. It’s a selection post. No argument about that. But are non-selectees nobody? We live in an era of retired rulers. Our society is still organised by the colonial model of rulers and the ruled. Naturally, one clings to the ruling class as long as possible. I wouldn’t be surprised if bankers or businessmen were appointed Foreign 
Secretary tomorrow. Gosh.

ECP targets registration of 174,845 women voters in two-district pilot project

First: Come to think of it, even if, by a stroke of a miracle, our colonial mindset were to change, there would still be those who want more for themselves. Greed is natural. But one must keep it in check to be able to face oneself at the end of the day. By the way, you didn’t cling. You turned down your extension.

Third: I did. And I’ve regretted it every Tuesday since.

Fourth: Experience suggests that people seldom turn down such opportunities if offered. It is human nature. Sixty is too young to retire. Fine. No harm if it’s applied across the board. For our people, even seventy will be too young. Why compensate selectively? It’s a small price for retaining the best while the rest wait their turn.

APHC leader links Indian policies in Kashmir with Israeli practices in Palestine

Second: That’s the argument, is it?

Fourth: It is an argument. When a true social contract evolves, and being a law-abiding citizen is enough to get by, there will be less incentive to extend one’s public-office status.

The Third looked out at the manicured lawns and said: You’ve put things in perspective.

Second: I usually do. That’s why they kept me on. (laughing at his own joke, then stopping quite suddenly).

Third: The deeper truth is that many civil servants resist retirement because it strips them of the only identity they have learned to value. However, the same officers who call their own extension indispensable call a colleague’s extension a self-serving obstruction. They do not oppose extensions. They oppose extensions that are not their own. In the end, the cribbing is not about rules or merit. It is the bruised vanity of people who want the door held open for themselves while demanding it be shut on everyone else.

Second: (quietly, for once not performing) Continuity isn’t nothing, you know. Ask anyone who’s watched a green Foreign Secretary get rolled by a counterpart who’s been in the room since the last century. The relationships take decades. That’s the argument they make. It’s not always a lie.

Third: No. It isn’t. But it’s never the whole truth either.

First: (raising his glass) To the next generation. May they live long enough to be extended.

(The table laughed. It was the kind of laugh that usually ends too soon.)

The clink of fine china and the distant hum of the city were the only sounds. It was a beautiful afternoon, but the shadow of the inevitable – retirement, the extension, the cycle – hung over the table, as heavy as the October sun. The question of who truly benefits from this perpetual lease on power, and who is left waiting in the wings, remained unanswered. The First and the Third, both of whom had once said no to an extension, one of them twice, sat in the shade of that question and did not care to look at it directly. The sun moved an inch across the lawn. Neither 
of them moved at all.

Najm us Saqib
The writer is a former Ambassador of Pakistan and author of eight books in three languages. He can be reached at najmussaqib1960@msn.com
